newsitem.title: FINLAND: UPM SEEN FOCUSED ON REPAP LWC MILL.
newsitem.headline: UPM SEEN FOCUSED ON REPAP LWC MILL.

text.p: Finnish UPM-Kymmene -- the world's biggest producer of coated magazine papers -- is likely to bid for Canadian Repap's light-weight-coated (LWC) magazine paper mill, but not the whole company, analysts said on Monday.

UPM has said it showed an interest in parts of financially troubled Repap last year, and speculation that it may buy some or all of the firm was revived last week when a takeover bid by Canada's Avenor failed.
Repap then said it would consider bids for its parts, and aimed to conclude the process by the third quarter.
Avenor bid C$2.6 billion (9.6 billion markka) for all of Repap but analysts said it was very unlikely that UPM would make a similar offer.
"There is no way UPM would be interested in buying all of Repap," said Postipankki analyst Niina Aikas.
At Opstock, analyst Jukka Linden said: "UPM is probably most interested in Repap's LWC paper production."
Repap's 1995 annual report showed it has a LWC mill in New Brunswick with annual capacity of 492,000 tonnes on two machines.
It also has a mill in Wisconsin with three paper machines producing a full range of coated paper rolls and sheets, bringing its full coated paper capacity to one million tonnes.

A brand new complete LWC production line including one 300,000-tonne machine would cost close to one billion markka ($200 million), of which the machine alone would make up about 500 million ($100 million), an official at Finnish paper machine maker Valmet Oy told Reuters.

Repap also has a 170,000-tonne superior strength kraft paper mill in Manitoba and many sawmills; plus it produces 685,000 tonnes of northern bleached softwood kraft pulp and 125,000 tonnes of magnesium-bisulphate hardwood pulp.

According to Finnish industry data, Repap is number eight in the world in coated magazine papers, clearly behind world leader UPM whose coated magazine paper capacity is set to rise to 2.2 million tonnes this year from 1.83 million currently.
Measured by market capitalisation, Repap is much smaller than UPM.

Its current market capitalisation is about C$105 (386 million markka, $75 million). UPM, the world's fourth largest forest industry group and the biggest outside North America, has market capitalisation of 30.63 billion markka ($5.94 billion).
Repap is also struggling with a C$2.4 billion (8.8 billion markka, $1.7 billion) debt load and losses.
Dennis Christie at Kleinwort Benson in London said he expected UPM to examine very closely any possible purchase and buy no more than four paper machines, if any.

"I don't think UPM would buy something unless they found it has good value," Christie said, adding that UPM does have scope to invest some four to five billion markka ($0.8-1.0 billion), for instance by selling non-core assets.
UPM's 59.5 percent stake in engineering group Rauma is worth 3.5 billion markka ($680 million), but it has said it will look to keep a significant minority stake.
Christie said Rauma shares were, however, a highly unlikely form of UPM payment for Repap's machines.
"I don't see anybody in North America selling a paper machine in exchange for Rauma shares," he said.

Analysts said UPM also has some cash from selling a cardboard plant, a chemical industry operation and shares in Finnish power producer Pohjolan Voima, but they were not clear how much. UPM has not announced any major investments this year.
